abstract: Over the past decade, metabolomic research in livestock and poultry has gained considerable momentum; however, quail metabolomics still lags behind that of livestock species such as chickens, pigs, and cattle. Quails are important models due to their low-cost protein sources—both eggs and meat—and practical benefits such as minimal space requirements, high egg production, disease resistance, and rapid reproduction. Therefore, it is necessary to systematically understand the effects of various factors on quail metabolism to provide a theoretical basis for accurate feeding and breeding practices. In this study, liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectroscopy (LC-MS/MS)-based metabolomics was used to examine the effects of age, breed, and sex on the serum metabolic profile of quails. A total of 550 metabolites were identified. Relative to breed and sex, we found that age played a crucial role in influencing quail serum metabolites. At 20 days of age (D20), quails had high levels of serum thymidine and alpha-D-glucose, while at 70 days of age (D70), the lipids, including 3-isothujone, 15-deoxy-d-12,14-PGJ2, and 2-aminobut-2-enoate dominated the serum. Additionally, xanthine, hypoxanthine, diaminopimelic acid, and 2-deoxy-scyllo-inosose appeared to be specific metabolites of Japanese quail (JAPQ). Serum levels of N-acetylglutamic acid, hydroxypyruvic acid, carnosine, alloepipregnanolone, lumichrome, 6-hydroxynicotinate, and myristic acid were higher in D70 Hengyan white feather quails (HYWQ) than those in D70 JAPQ. Notably, this study also identified 2-hydroxy-2-ethylsuccinic acid and riboflavin as potential specific metabolites in female quails. Furthermore, integration analysis showed that amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism, as well as ABC transporters, were the key pathways distinguishing D20 from D70. Purine metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, ABC transporters, and TCA cycle were the key pathways distinguishing HYWQ from JAPQ. Differences in energy metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism were observed between males and females. These findings enhance our understanding of the dynamic changes in quail serum metabolites influenced by various factors and address the knowledge gap regarding serum metabolic changes at different stages in quails.

Materials and methods
Ethics statement
This study was conducted under the Chinese guidelines for animal welfare. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee (ACUC) of Nanchang Normal University.
Animals and sample collection
A total of 40 quail samples (JAPQ, n = 20; HYWQ, n = 20) obtained from Jiangxi Hengyan Poultry Co. Ltd. (Fengcheng, Jiangxi, China) were used for this experiment. Based on previous research (
Madekurozwa, 2014
), the quails selected for the study were aged 20 and 70 days, with an equal number of males and females. The quails were housed under identical environmental and nutritional conditions, and freshwater was provided
ad libitum
. Blood samples were collected from the quail wing veins and centrifuged at a speed of 2,000g/min for 15 min to obtain serum samples. These samples were then frozen with liquid nitrogen and eventually stored at −80°C until subsequent metabolomic analyses.
Serum untargeted metabolomic analysis
All frozen serum samples were initially thawed at 4°C. After the samples had completely thawed, 100 μL of quail serum was transferred into a 2 mL EP tube, cold methanol was added four times; the mixture was thoroughly mixed using a vortex. This was followed by centrifugation at 12000 g and 4°C for 10 min. The supernatant was transferred into a new EP tube, concentrated and dried in a vacuum centrifugal concentrator, and then 150 μL of 80 % methanol solution of 2-chlorobenzalanine was added to redissolve the precipitate. The supernatant was separated and filtered for LC-MS analysis.
Liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectroscopy analysis and data processing
Liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectroscopy (LC–MS) analysis was conducted using a Thermo Ultimate 3000 UHPLC system coupled with Thermo Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer at Suzhou PANOMIX Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd. Metabolite separation was performed using ACQUITY UPLC® HSS T3 1.8 μm column (2.1 × 150 mm, Waters). The mass spectrum signals were acquired in both positive and negative modes using electrospray ionization. Gradient elution was performed using two different solutions: formic acid in water (1 %) and formic acid in acetonitrile (1 %) or ammonium formate in water and acetonitrile solution. In the electrospray ionization series mass spectrometry, the positive ion spray voltage and negative ion spray voltage were 3.5 kV and −2.5 kV, respectively. The analyzer was set up for full scan in the m/z range of 81-1000 Da. Finally, the MS/MS second-level scans were performed using data-dependent scanning.
Metabolites were identified based on accurate mass (m/z, 10 ppm), retention time, and spectral patterns by searching an in-house library of chemical standards and a manually curated list of public databases such as MoNA (
https://mona.fiehnlab.ucdavis.edu
), mzCloud (
https://www.mzcloud.org
), and METLIN (
http://metlin.scripps.edu
) were also used for metabolite identification using accurate mass, isotope patterns, and MS/MS spectra. The following criteria must be met for metabolite identification: narrow retention time, accurate
m
/
z
values
<
10 ppm, and MS/MS spectra with high forward and reverse scores.
Statistical analysis
Multivariate statistical analyses of serum metabolomic data, including principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were used to determine overall metabolic changes and the repeatability and stability of obtained models. The score plot was visualized, and the variable importance in projection (VIP) values were determined using OPLS-DA, and used to filter out the signals irrelevant to model classification by eliminating noise in the data that was irrelevant to classification. Significantly different metabolites were identified based on the combination of a statistically significant VIP values obtained from the OPLS-DA model and the
P
-value obtained from 2-tailed Student's t-tests (Beijing Stats Data Mining Co. Ltd, Beijing, China) conducted on the raw data. VIP > 1.00,
P
< 0.05, fold changes (FC) ≥ 1.5, or FC ≤ 0.667, were considered as significantly different metabolites. Pathways associated with the biomarkers were described using databases Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG;
http://www.kegg.com
). Volcano plots and Lollipop chart were performed using the Metware Cloud online platform. Cluster heatmaps was generated using the R software with the “ggplot2” and “heatmap” packages.
body:
Introduction
Simple factors such as sex, age, and breed have proven valuable in determining livestock productivity. The dynamic energy requirements and metabolic characteristics of the different breeds and growth stages of livestock and poultry provide important guidance for breed selection and precision feeding strategies. Although the molecular mechanisms are not yet fully understood, researchers have long used information from livestock and poultry phenotypes to carry out extensive breeding (
Elkhaiat et al., 2023
;
Ibrahim et al., 2021
).
Quails are favored by consumers in various countries as a low-cost source of animal protein, providing both eggs and meat; this is because they require comparatively little space for feeding and rearing, lay many eggs, are highly resistant to avian diseases, and reproduce quickly (
Molino et al., 2015
). Hence, quails are also commonly used as laboratory animal models in scientific research (
Huss et al., 2008
;
Lyte et al., 2021
). Traditional livestock and poultry breeds have long breeding cycles and often require several generations to set up a successful breeding program. However, with the development of multi-omics technologies, such as genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, along with the advancements of molecular breeding techniques, the breeding cycle has been greatly shortened. Metabolomics is a widely used strategy for analyzing small-molecule metabolites that can directly influence phenotypes (
Chen et al., 2023
). In recent years, metabolomics has gained significant usage and popularity in animal studies. For example, studies have identified the differences in meat quality between Shitou and Wuzhong geese (
Chen et al., 2024
), revealed potential biomarkers for small yellow follicles in chickens during sexual maturation (
Zhao et al., 2023
), and documented age-dependent dynamic changes in chicken meat (
Li et al., 2022
).
In chickens, it is well established that age and sex affect the infection and treatment of diseases (
Ngongolo & Chota, 2022
). Significant changes occur in the endocrine and other physiological states of birds during sexual development. To date, studies on quail metabolomics have been relatively limited compared to those of other domestic animals. Our previous study found significant alterations in serum metabolites related to microorganisms between before and after sexual maturity groups in 22 quails (
Xiong et al., 2023b
). However, the effects of breed, age, and sex on quail serum metabolism remain unclear. In the present study, 40 serum samples were collected from two breeds (Hengyan white feather quail (HYWQ) and Japanese quail (JAPQ)) at two different ages (D20 and D70), with an equal number of males and females. Untargeted metabolomic profiles of these host serum samples were comprehensively measured to study the effects of age, breed, and sex on the metabolic network of quails. Identifying these metabolites is expected to help monitor and evaluate the physiological state and nutritional level of quails, providing a theoretical basis for accurate feeding and breeding.
Materials and methods
Ethics statement
This study was conducted under the Chinese guidelines for animal welfare. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee (ACUC) of Nanchang Normal University.
Animals and sample collection

Madekurozwa, 2014
), the quails selected for the study were aged 20 and 70 days, with an equal number of males and females. The quails were housed under identical environmental and nutritional conditions, and freshwater was provided
ad libitum
. Blood samples were collected from the quail wing veins and centrifuged at a speed of 2,000g/min for 15 min to obtain serum samples. These samples were then frozen with liquid nitrogen and eventually stored at −80°C until subsequent metabolomic analyses.

Metabolites were identified based on accurate mass (m/z, 10 ppm), retention time, and spectral patterns by searching an in-house library of chemical standards and a manually curated list of public databases such as MoNA (
https://mona.fiehnlab.ucdavis.edu
), mzCloud (
https://www.mzcloud.org
), and METLIN (
http://metlin.scripps.edu
) were also used for metabolite identification using accurate mass, isotope patterns, and MS/MS spectra. The following criteria must be met for metabolite identification: narrow retention time, accurate
m
/
z
values
<
10 ppm, and MS/MS spectra with high forward and reverse scores.
Statistical analysis
Multivariate statistical analyses of serum metabolomic data, including principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were used to determine overall metabolic changes and the repeatability and stability of obtained models. Significantly different metabolites were identified based on the combination of a statistically significant VIP values obtained from the OPLS-DA model and the
P
-value obtained from 2-tailed Student's t-tests (Beijing Stats Data Mining Co. Ltd, Beijing, China) conducted on the raw data. VIP > 1.00,
P
< 0.05, fold changes (FC) ≥ 1.5, or FC ≤ 0.667, were considered as significantly different metabolites. Pathways associated with the biomarkers were described using databases Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG;
http://www.kegg.com
). Volcano plots and Lollipop chart were performed using the Metware Cloud online platform. Cluster heatmaps was generated using the R software with the “ggplot2” and “heatmap” packages.
Results
Serum metabolic profiles in quails
In this study, non-targeted LC–MS/MS metabolomics was performed using serum samples from 40 quails. After data preprocessing and metabolite identification, a total of 1651 metabolites (MS1) were detected, and a total of 550 metabolites (MS2) were identified based on second-order MS matching scores (Supplementary Table S1). Entry for each metabolite included essential information such as the metabolite name, m/z ratio, retention time, molecular formula, exact mass, and library reference. MS1 and MS2 were distinguished based on the metabolite identification significance score including identify and
P
-value obtained from
m
/
z
values and MS/MS spectra scores.
Age-related effects on serum metabolite profiles of quails
Using the 550 identified metabolites, we explored the differences in metabolites between D20 and D70 using multivariate statistical analysis. First, unsupervised PCA was performed to visualize clusters and decrease the data dimensions. The PCA score plots of the serum metabolomic data showed a clear separation with no overlap for each group, suggesting that the metabolites changed significantly between D20 and D70 in both quail breeds, HYWQ (
Fig. 1
A) and JAPQ (
Fig. 1
B). Subsequently, we performed OPLS-DA to further differentiate the metabolite features and to screen potential marker metabolites; the model revealed a clear distinction between D20 and D70 (
Fig. 2
A and B). For cross-validation, the parameters explained variation (R2Y) = 0.996/0.992 and prediction capability (Q2) = 0.926/0.919, demonstrated good cumulative interpretation ability and predictive power of models (
Fig. 2
C and D).
Fig. 1
Principal component analysis (PCA) score plots of the serum metabolites in Hengyan white feather and Japanese quails. (A) B20 vs B70. (B) C20 vs C70. (C) B20 vs C20. (D) B70 vs C70. (E) B70M vs B70F. (A) C70M vs C70F. B20: D20 Hengyan white feather quails; C20: D20 Japanese quails; B70: D70 Hengyan white feather quails; C70: D70 Japanese quails. B70F: D70 female Hengyan white feather quails; B70M: D70 male Hengyan white feather quails; C70F: D70 female Japanese quails; C70M: D70 male Hengyan white feather quails. Each dot represents an individual sample of quail (n = 5 or 10).
Fig 1
Fig. 2
Orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) score plots comparing D20 and D70 quails. (A) and (C) B20 vs B70. (B) and (D) C20 vs C70. B20: D20 Hengyan white feather quails; B70: D70 Hengyan white feather quails; C20: D20 Japanese quails; C70: D70 Japanese quails. Each dot represents an individual sample of quail (n = 10).
Fig 2
Based on the OPLS-DA analysis, we screened for differential metabolites in quail serum between D20 and D70 using the following criteria: with VIP > 1.0,
P
< 0.05, and FC > 1.5, or FC < 0.667, and used volcano plots to detect differential metabolites. The volcano plots show the abundance of differential metabolites between D20 and D70 in HYWQ (
Fig. 3
A). Compared to metabolites in HYWQ on D70, 79 metabolites were up regulated, and 124 were down regulated in HYWQ on D20. We identified 97 significantly down regulated and 79 up regulated differential metabolites in JAPQ on D20 compared to those in JAPQ on D70 (
Fig. 3
B). To further understand the changes of different metabolites at different ages, we generated a lollipop chart for the top 40 differential metabolites ranked by log2FC (
Fig. 3
C and D). Notably, the different metabolites from the two breeds overlapped between D20 and D70. The upregulated metabolites included pyrrolidonecarboxylic acid, 3-isothujone, 5,6-dihydrothymine, 15-deoxy-d-12,14-PGJ2, 1,2,3-trihydroxybenzene, 2-aminobut-2-enoate and catechol, and the down-regulated metabolites included 2-methyl-3-oxopropanoic acid, alpha-D-glucose, indolepyruvate, and thymidine.
Fig. 3
Overview of differential metabolites and the top 20 Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways in serum metabolomics at different ages in Japanese quails (JAPQ) and Hengyan white feather quails (HYWQ). (A) Volcano plot for differential metabolites between D20 HYWQ and D70 HYWQ. (B) Volcano plot for differential metabolites between D20 JAPQ and D70 JAPQ. (C) Lollipop chart of the top 40 metabolites (based on log2FC) between D20 HYWQ and D70 HYWQ. (D) Lollipop chart of the top 20 metabolites (based on log2FC) between D20 JAPQ and D70 JAPQ. The top 20 KEGG pathways were identified from the age-differential accumulated metabolites (DAMs) in the serum metabolome of HYWQ (E) and JAPQ (F). FC: fold changes; VIP: variable importance in projection.
Fig 3
Finally, the KEGG database was used to analyze differential metabolites and obtain metabolism-related pathways between D20 and D70, which may potentially be associated with the mobilization and repartitioning of nutrients and energy during quail growth and development (
Fig. 3
E and F). Different metabolites were enriched in pathways including phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis, tyrosine metabolism, beta-alanine metabolism, aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, histidine metabolism, phenylalanine metabolism, butanoate metabolism, and D-glutamine and D-glutamate metabolism.
Breed-related effects on serum metabolite profiles of quails
To further examine the differences between the two breeds, PCA was performed according to age. As shown in
Figs. 1
C and D, the PCA plots of the serum metabolomic data showed clear separation with no overlap between each group. Compared to D20, the separation of the two varieties at D70 was greater. In the OPLS-DA score plot, there were clear differences between the JAPQ and HWFQ breeds (
Fig. 4
A and B). When R2Y and Q2 values > 0.5 and >0.9, respectively, the OPLS-DA models were not over-fitted and had good predictive ability, and the metabolome data were reliable (
Fig. 4
C and D).
Fig. 4
Orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) score plots comparing HYWQ and JAPQ. (A) and (C) B20 vs C20. (B) and (D) B70 vsC70. B20: D20 Hengyan white feather quails; B70: D70 Hengyan white feather quails; C20: D20 Japanese quails; C70: D70 Japanese quails. Each dot represents an individual sample of quail (n = 10).
Fig 4
Using the VIP scores derived from the OPLS-DA models, differentially accumulated metabolites were screened under the conditions of VIP > 1,
P
< 0.05, and FC > 1.5 or FC < 0.667. Differential metabolites were found in the serum of quails at D20 and D70 from different varieties and plotted volcano plots for all detected differential metabolites (
Fig. 5
A and B). Based on pairwise comparisons of HYWQ and JAPQ, 29 metabolites were significantly up regulated and 48 were down regulated in the serum at D20. Similarly, 52 metabolites were up regulated, and 36 were down regulated at D70. The highest number of differential metabolites progressively increased with age. In contrast to their concentration in JAPQ, the concentrations of cadaverine, 4-acetamidobutanoic acid, 3-methyl-l-tyrosine, thymidine, d-arabitol, acetaminophen, 3-methylthiopropionic acid, benzoate, m-chlorophenylpiperazine (m-cpp), and nitrobenzene were upregulated in HYWQ at D20. The concentrations of N-acetylglutamic acid, hydroxypyruvic acid, carnosine, 5-hydroxymethyl-2-furancarboxaldehyde, alloepipregnanolone, lumichrome, 6-hydroxynicotinate, myristic acid, nitrendipine, and L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid were upregulated in HYWQ at D70 (
Fig. 5
C and D). Some metabolites showed opposite trends in these two quail breeds, such as lumichrome, 6-hydroxynicotinate, cytidine, D-fructose, and D-synephrine, which were upregulated at D20 in JAPQ and at D70 in HYWQ; 3-methylthiopropionic acid, vanillylmandelic acid, and ectoine were upregulated at D20 in HYWQ and at D70 in JAPQ. Moreover, we horizontally compared all differential metabolites of the two breeds, and found that xanthine, hypoxanthine, diaminopimelic acid and 2-deoxy-scyllo-inosose in JAPQ were up regulated at both D20 and D70 compared to those in HYWQ (
Fig. 5
A and B). Finally, by integrating the correlations of differential metabolites with KEGG analysis, we summarized and manually constructed the metabolite-pathway interaction networks in the serum. As shown in
Fig. 5
E, at D20, most metabolic pathways were involved in amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, and energy metabolism. More specifically, this included aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, arginine and proline metabolism, tyrosine metabolism, beta-alanine metabolism, purine metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, and pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis. At D70, most metabolic pathways were involved in amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism and energy metabolism, including glycine, serine and threonine metabolism, phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, cysteine and methionine metabolism, and citrate cycle (
Fig. 5
F).
Fig. 5
Overview of differential metabolites and the top 20 Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways in serum metabolomics across different breeds. (A) Volcano plot for differential metabolites between B20 and C20. (B) Volcano plot for differential metabolites between B70 and C70. (C) Lollipop chart of the top 20 metabolites (based on log2FC) between B20 and C20. (D) Lollipop chart of the top 20 metabolites (based on log2FC) between B70 and C70. The top 20 KEGG pathways were identified from the breed-differential accumulated metabolites (DAMs) in the serum metabolome of day 20 (E) and day 70 (F). FC: fold changes; VIP: variable importance in projection. B20: D20 Hengyan white feather quails; B70: D70 Hengyan white feather quails; C20: D20 Japanese quails; C70: D70 Japanese quails.
Fig 5
Sex-related effects on serum metabolite profiles of quails
Considering that the effect of sex was not negligible, we further analyzed the metabolite network between males and females at D70 in both breeds. To better understand the metabolic differences between female and male quails, PCA and OPLS-DA were applied for pairwise comparisons. When comparing HYWQ females and males, PCA explained 19.9 % and 14.5 % of the total variation, respectively (
Fig. 1
E). Similarly, in the comparison of JAPQ females and males, PCA explained 20.0 % and 14.7 % of the total variation, respectively (
Fig. 1
F). The OPLS-DA models were expressed as R2Y and Q2 > 0.5 (
Fig. 6
), suggesting that metabolites changed significantly between males and females.
Fig. 6
Orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) score plot comparing females and males. B70F: D70 female Hengyan white feather quails; B70M: D70 male Hengyan white feather quails; C70F: D70 female Japanese quails; C70M: D70 male Hengyan white feather quails. Each dot represents an individual sample of quail (n = 5).
Fig 6
To identify metabolites that significantly contributed to the separation of the two sexes, we selected metabolites with VIP > 1.0,
P
< 0.05, and FC > 1.5, or FC < 0.667 as the threshold values. A total of 48 metabolites met these criteria in HYWQ, and in JAPQ, 31 metabolites met the criteria, with similar metabolic networks between the two breeds. Compared with males, 2-hydry-2-ethylsni acid and riboflavin were down regulated, and biliverdin was up regulated in females (
Fig. 7
A and B). In HYWQ, the top 10 candidate biomarkers, namely 4-methylaminobutyrate, phosphocreatine, thymidine, biliverdin, 3-dehydroshikimate, kojic acid, 2-pyrrolidinone, beta-glycerophosphoric acid, baciofen, and 3-methoxyanthranilate were up regulated in males compared with females. Conversely, riboflavin, 2-hydroxy-2-ethylsuccinic acid, androsterone glucuronide, maleic acid, itaconic acid, fumaric acid, CDP-ethanolamine, m-cresol, 1,2,3-trihydroxybenzene, and D-glucose were down regulated in male quails compared to females. Regarding the differential metabolites between females and males from JAPQ, glycochenodeoxycholic acid, picolinic acid, tyrosol, xanthine, xanthosine, baclofen, acetyl-maltose, carnosine, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, and 3-indoleacetonitrile were among the top10 metabolites in male quails. In contrast, 2-hydroxy-2-ethylsuccinic acid, riboflavin, D-xylitol, 1-aminocyclopropanecarboxylic acid, delta-12-pProstaglandin J2, 2-oxo-4-methylthiobutanoic acid, norethindrone, chavicol, triethylamine, and dodecanedioic acid were the top10 metabolites in female quails.
Fig. 7
Overview of differential metabolites and the top 20 Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways in serum metabolomics between different sex. (A) Volcano plot for differential metabolites between B70M and B70F. (B) Volcano plot for differential metabolites between C70F and C70M. (C) Lollipop chart of the top 20 metabolites (based on log2FC) between B70M and B70F. (D) Lollipop chart of the top 20 metabolites (based on log2FC) between B70F and B70M. The top 20 KEGG pathways were identified from the breed-differential accumulated metabolites (DAMs) in the serum metabolome of D20 (E) and D70 (F). FC: fold changes; VIP: variable importance in projection. B70F: D70 female Hengyan white feather quails; B70M: D70 male Hengyan white feather quails; C70F: D70 female Japanese quails; C70M: D70 male Hengyan white feather quails.
Fig 7
The biological functions of the differentially expressed were determined using KEGG pathway analysis.
Fig. 7
E and F showed the top 20 enriched pathways in each comparison group. The results indicated that the differential metabolites between males and female HYWQ were enriched in pathways that were more inclined toward amino acid metabolism and carbohydrate metabolism pathways (e.g., citrate cycle, pentose phosphate pathway, insulin signaling pathway, and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis). However, JAPQ was more inclined towards amino acid metabolism and lipid metabolism (arachidonic acid metabolism and sphingolipid metabolism). The sex-differentiated metabolites of the two breeds covered the same metabolic pathways, including tyrosine metabolism, alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, tryptophan metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, arginine biosynthesis, riboflavin metabolism, and ABC transporters.
Discussion
Over the past decade, metabolomic research in livestock and poultry has gained considerable momentum; however, quail metabolomics still lags behind the study of livestock species such as chickens, pigs, and cattle (
Gu et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Su et al., 2022
). Most previous studies have focused on the metabolic regulation of quails due to nutrient or toxic exposure, ignoring the effects of factors such as breeds, age, and sex (
Bonagurio et al., 2020
;
Han et al., 2023
). Therefore, we characterized quail metabolome and identified the influences of breed, age, and sex. These results enrich the catalogue of metabolites in quail serum.
A total of 550 metabolites were identified in serum samples from quails at two different breeds, at two different developmental stages, and both sexes through a comparative analysis of serum metabolomes. At D20, quails had high levels of serum thymidine and alpha-D-glucose, which may be necessary for growth and development. At D70, the markers were mainly lipids, including 3-isothujone, 15-deoxy-D-12,14-PGJ2, and 2-aminobut-2-enoate, which may be associated with increased body fat and fatty acid synthesis with increasing age. Moreover, 15-deoxy-D-12,14-PGJ2 is a natural peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPAR-γ) agonist that triggers the PPAR-γ signaling pathway (
Li et al., 2019
). The content of pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, which is associated with proline metabolism, was higher at D70. Proline plays crucial roles in protein synthesis and structure, metabolism, and nutrition, as well as wound healing, antioxidative reactions, and immune responses. Although most mammals can synthesize proline from arginine and glutamine/glutamate, the rate of endogenous synthesis is inadequate in neonates, birds, and fish (
Wu et al., 2011
). Therefore, compared with D70 quails, D20 quails require more proline to meet their metabolic requirements. Breed differences also significantly affect serum metabolites (
Tian et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2023
). Our KEGG analysis showed that the differential metabolites between D20 and D70 in the two breeds were significantly enriched in aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis, which is essential for amino acid biosynthesis(
Wang et al., 2018
). We also observed that amino acid metabolism pathways, such as phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis, tyrosine metabolism, beta-alanine metabolism, arginine biosynthesis, histidine metabolism, and phenylalanine metabolism were the main metabolic pathways enriched with differential metabolites related to age. The amino acid metabolism positively impacts growth performance and health status in poultry (
Fathima et al., 2023
;
He et al., 2021
). The differential regulation of these metabolites, along with the involvement of amino acid metabolism pathways, may reflect differences between D20 and D70. Consequently, these metabolic pathways have the potential to serve as biomarkers for distinguishing the different stages of quail development.
We found that xanthine, hypoxanthine, diaminopimelic acid (DAP) and 2-deoxy-scyllo-inosose may be specific metabolites of the JAPQ. Hypoxanthine and xanthine can be oxidized to produce uric acid, which is the primary nitrogenous excretory product in birds. Although hypoxanthine and xanthine have been used as important markers for many diseases in mammals, they have also been shown to promote quail and chick myoblast proliferation in vitro (
Ichio et al., 1985
). Diaminopimelic acid is a lysine-like amino acid derivative that is a key component of the bacterial cell wall, and bacteria can synthesize L-lysine from aspartate and pyruvate via the DAP pathway (
Liu et al., 2021
;
Styriak et al., 1992
). This process may be closely related to the gut microbes in JAPQ (
Xiong et al., 2023a
). By comparing the metabolites between D20 and D70 in JAPQ, we found that the top 20 different metabolites in serum at D20 mainly included amino acid metabolites such as L-histidine, 2-ketobutyric acid, L-tryptophan, 1-methylhistidine, L-kynurenine, and beta-alanyl-L-arginine, which are primarily involved in tryptophan metabolism and histidine metabolism. Histidine and tryptophan are essential amino acids in poultry. In addition to protein anabolism, histidine is a particularly important limiting factor in carnosine synthesis and has strong anti-oxidant effects (
Moro et al., 2020
). Tryptophan affects hormone secretion, immune organ development, meat and egg production, and meat and egg quality in poultry raised under controlled or stressed conditions (
Fouad et al., 2021
). Furthermore, the top 20 different metabolites in the serum at D70 in the JAPQ included energy metabolites (e.g., 6-phosphogluconic acid, phosphocreatine, and D-ribose). 6-phosphogluconic acid serves as a metabolic intermediate in the pentose phosphate pathway, which is crucial for nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis, redox homoeostasis, and biosynthetic processes (
TeSlaa et al., 2023
). Phosphocreatine is a phosphorylated creatine molecule that serves as a rapidly mobilizable reserve of high-energy phosphates for recycling adenosine triphosphate. Guanidinoacetic acid, when added to the diet, promotes growth through its main metabolite creatine (
Portocarero & Braun, 2021
). Nevertheless, the serum levels of N-acetylglutamic acid (NAG), hydroxypyruvic acid, carnosine, alloepipregnanolone, lumichrome, 6-hydroxynicotinate, and myristic acid (MA) in D70 HYWQ were higher than those in D70 JAPQ. N-acetylglutamic acid is involved in arginine biosynthesis, which is increased in HYWQ (
Dai et al., 2024
). Carnosine may improve quail sperm quality (
Sarkar et al., 2021
) and dietary carnosine has been shown to improve intestinal immune responses and gut barrier function in broiler chickens (
Park et al., 2024
). Myristic acid plays a variety of roles in livestock and poultry, such as providing energy, participating in the synthesis of fatty acids (
Zhou et al., 2023
), promoting lipid synthesis by activating SREBP through the mTOR signaling pathway (
Chu et al., 2022
), and exerting anti-inflammatory activity through the NF-κB pathway (
Huang et al., 2023
). Quail meat is considered an important protein resource with a high amino acid profile, similar to other poultry, which is of high biological significance due to the proportion of non-essential and essential amino acids (1.35:1) (
Nasr et al., 2017
). This explains why KEGG analysis showed that aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis and amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism were the main metabolic pathways in quails. However, different stages of development have different metabolic needs; the differential metabolites between HYWQ and JAPQ at D20 were significantly enriched in purine metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, and mTOR signaling pathway. In contrast, the differential metabolites between HYWQ and JAPQ at D70 were significantly enriched in ABC transporters, citrate cycle, and glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism.
We analyzed the top 10 differential metabolites between D70 male and female quails, and found that 2-hydroxy-2-ethylsuccinic acid and riboflavin may be specific metabolites in female quails. Riboflavin is a precursor of flavin mononucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide, which are cofactors for many energetic enzymes and can protect cells from oxidative damage (
Saedisomeolia & Ashoori, 2018
). Previous studies have suggested that riboflavin is particularly important for the reproductive performance of male animals (
Kuang et al., 2021
). Wild-type mice treated with a riboflavin-deficient diet may exhibit morphological and bioenergetic defects in spermatozoa because insufficient riboflavin transport into the mitochondrial matrix suppresses oxidative phosphorylation and reprograms spermatozoa energy metabolism by disrupting flavoenzyme functions through
SLC22A14
(
Kuang et al., 2021
). This may contribute to the observed difference in riboflavin levels in the extracellular fluid between sexes. In addition, we found that male and female HYWQ metabolites were mainly enriched in amino acid metabolism and carbohydrate metabolism, while JAPQ were more likely involved in amino acid metabolism and lipid metabolism. It is widely accepted that female sexual maturity is particularly affected by energy metabolism, which relies on the mobilization of stored carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins (
Fontana & Della Torre, 2016
). This may be related to the maintenance of egg laying performance in female quails.
Conclusions
In summary, a total of 550 metabolites were identified in quail serum. Relative to breed and sex, we found that age played a crucial role in influencing quail serum metabolites. Serum levels of thymidine and alpha-D-glucose were higher in quail at D20, whereas lipids such as 3-isothujone, 15-deoxy-d-12,14-PGJ2, and 2-aminobut-2-enoate were higher at D70. Additionally, xanthine, hypoxanthine, diaminopimelic acid, and 2-deoxy-scyllo-inosose appeared to be specific to JAPQ. Furthermore, 2-hydroxy-2-ethylsuccinic acid and riboflavin may be specific to female quails. Integration analysis revealed that amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism and ABC transporters were the key pathways between D20 and D70. Purine metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, ABC transporters, and citrate cycle were the key pathways distinguishing HYWQ from JAPQ. Energy metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism were the differential pathways between the males and females. The results of this study illustrate the dynamic changes in serum metabolites across different ages, breeds and sexes of quails, filling a gap in understanding serum metabolic changes at different developmental stages. However, this study also had a few limitations. For example, our results were based on changes in serum metabolites, associations with phenotype analysis, and potential regulatory mechanisms that have not yet been elucidated. Future studies are needed to verify the functions of metabolites in conjunction with phenotypic data to better inform breed selection and precision feeding of quails.
